text: Rudi Dekkers (July 27, 1956 – April 11, 2024) was a Dutch businessman and convicted drug trafficker. He was the former owner of Huffman Aviation, a flight school in Venice, Florida, and gained worldwide attention after the September 11 attacks when it was revealed that he had trained two of the hijackers—Mohamed Atta and Marwan al-Shehhi—who crashed American Airlines Flight 11 and United Airlines Flight 175 into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center. Born in Apeldoorn, The Netherlands, Dekkers grew up in the Jordaan neighborhood of Amsterdam, where he lived in an abusive home and often ran away at age eight. He worked as a housing broker in Ede, selling three to four houses a week, and in 1983 met Bill Gates at a computer conference, which inspired him to establish a computer business in the Netherlands via Miami to bypass tax authorities, becoming one of the first computer dealers in the Netherlands. While working in real estate and the computer business, he obtained his pilot's license at Teuge Airport. In 1993, he moved to Florida after a tax fraud conviction that was later acquitted on appeal and due to disputes with former business partners, who accused him of defrauding them of tens of thousands of guilder, and a sexual harassment allegation from a former female employee that was settled. By 2001, Dekkers estimated his net worth at $12 million; he owned a Dodge Viper, a helicopter, and had a landing pad in front of his Naples, Florida, home. He purchased Huffman Aviation in 1999, which at the time had a fleet of 12 small aircraft and offered training in private pilot, instrument rating, commercial pilot license, multi-engine ratings, and flight instructor programs but not on larger jet aircraft. Atta and al-Shehhi trained at Huffman in July 2000 after meeting Dekkers during a coffee break in his office. In August, the school filed M-1 student visa requests for them to switch from tourist to student visas, which were granted on July 17, 2001, for Atta and August 9, 2001, for al-Shehhi, allowing enrollment in the pilot program from September 1, 2000, to September 1, 2001. During their training, both men lived with a company employee named Charlie Voss. After the attacks, the FBI investigated Huffman Aviation, seized records showing that Atta and al-Shehhi paid $10,000 for two months of flight instruction, and Dekkers cooperated fully with the FBI, with former investigator Kerry Myers stating he was "very cooperative" and that evidence linking Ramzi bin al-Shibh to the attacks came from Dekkers' records. Dekkers maintained he did not feel guilty, saying he had made copies of their passports and visas but saw no red flags, asserting "Nothing was out of the ordinary. We did our job." Following the attacks, Dekkers went bankrupt, lost his business and home, crashed a helicopter, and lost custody of his daughters; he received death threats and faced issues with the IRS, lenders, and the FAA. In January 2002, Huffman Aviation drew media attention when a reporter moved freely between cockpits and fuel tanks without being noticed, and in March, the school was cited for leaving fuel trucks unlocked with keys in the ignition at Venice Municipal Airport. On February 24, 2002, Dekkers suspected an assassination attempt when his helicopter crashed into the Caloosahatchee River after its fuel lines were cut. He criticized his lack of oversight at the school, but countered by blaming the U.S. lax border and visa systems, which he confirmed when he found two approved visa applications for Atta and al-Shehhi in March 2002. After the attacks, he lost $400,000 and most of his international students dropped out. A second school he operated in Naples was closed after he defaulted on loans, one of which was $1.7 million. Dekkers sold Huffman Aviation in 2003. In 2011, he stated that Atta and al-Shehhi "never displayed any behaviors that would have labeled them as terrorists" and that during training, they were nearly kicked out for not taking it seriously and being too busy fooling around; he described al-Shehhi as "a more likable person" who laughed and joked, while describing Atta as "dead man walking" due to his "white face and no emotions" and as "a nasty person, very unfriendly." Dekkers maintained he did not know what they would do and said he did not feel guilty, adding, "I don't feel guilty at all. I couldn't do nothing about it. I wish I could be a hero. I think about this often. Why me? But that's fate. You can't turn away from fate, I guess." In 2016, he stated his personal "9/11" began on September 12 when the FBI appeared at his business, saying, "For me, it's not an anniversary. I live 9/11 every day." In 2003, he established an air charter service in Naples, Florida, and by 2007, he was living in a villa in a gated community in Fort Myers, Florida, making a comfortable living selling swimming pools, remarried to a Cuban woman who was pregnant with their child. The 2008 financial crisis caused the collapse of the Florida housing market, leading him to lose his business; he then ran a cellphone store in Naples. By 2011, he was divorced again, in severe financial distress, with no job and facing eviction, living on food stamps, eating once a day, illegally tapping electricity, being chased by bailiffs, and having an expired U.S. visa, meaning he was in the country illegally. In 2011, he published an autobiography, Guilty by Association, detailing his life, passion for flying, and interactions with Atta and al-Shehhi. He praised the killing of Osama bin Laden, saying, "Like a lot of people, I wish I was the one. And bravo to everyone who was behind this. The head of the snake is gone." On December 2, 2012, Dekkers was arrested in Houston by U.S. Department of Homeland Security after accepting a blue suitcase containing 18.7 kilograms of cocaine and 860 grams of heroin; he was sentenced to five years in prison after one and a half years in pre-trial detention and was reportedly hospitalized after an assault by Mexican gang members. After his release, he moved to the Dominican Republic. On April 11, 2019, Dutch authorities arrested him at Amsterdam Airport Schiphol with 118 swallowed scoops of cocaine; he was sentenced to seven months in prison, two of which were suspended, but fled during a furlough abroad. He returned to the Netherlands in June 2022 and was ordered to serve two months of probation for cocaine smuggling, plus one month not served due to his flight. Dekkers was the subject of a 2021 three-part Dutch television documentary, Rudi - Achtervolgd door 9/11 (Rudi - Haunted by 9/11). In 2022, he lived in Medellín, Colombia, with his girlfriend Alexandra, and later moved to the Philippines, where he died from heart failure on April 11, 2024.
